title: Man charged with OUI, manslaughter in wrong-way crash that killed UNH hockey player - WFSB
content:
NORTH HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - State police have charged a 31-year-old man with manslaughter and other counts in an Oct. 16 wrong-way crash on Interstate 91 that killed University of New Haven student, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea. Troopers charged Guillermo Carmona-Lopez after obtaining an arrest warrant, police said. He was arrested Nov. 9 and arraigned from a hospital bed. Troopers responded to I-91 southbound near Exit 9 in North Haven for a report of a wrong-way crash, state police said. A preliminary investigation found O’Shea was driving a Honda Accord south in the left lane. Carmona-Lopez was driving a Chevrolet Silverado north in the southbound lanes and hit the Accord head-on, according to police. The Accord went into the left-center lane, where a Jeep Grand Cherokee hit it, police said. The Accord then went into the right lane and onto the right shoulder, where a GMC Terrain hit it. O’Shea was pronounced dead at the scene. Carmona-Lopez was taken to Yale New Haven Hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries, police said. The other drivers were hospitalized with minor injuries. State police said Carmona-Lopez’s license was suspended. One witness told police that as they neared the Exit 8 off-ramp, he saw headlights coming toward them. The witness said there was a car in the left lane approaching them, according to the account police recorded. Another witness captured the collision on a dash camera. Police said the video shows Carmona-Lopez’s truck drove toward and passed at least 18 vehicles before it struck O’Shea’s car. A trooper at the scene said Carmona-Lopez could not explain what happened and smelled of alcohol. Carmona-Lopez allegedly told police in an interview at the hospital that he drank four beers starting around 8 that night. He also said that once he got on the highway, he did not remember anything after that, according to the account police recorded. The arrest warrant states his blood alcohol level was .22 and .21. The legal limit is .08. He was held on $500,000 bond and had a bedside arraignment at the hospital Nov. 12. At last check, he remained in the custody of the state Department of Correction. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Carmona-Lopez is from Mexico and entered the country illegally. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him in May 2013 after he entered the country illegally. The agency said he was deported, then reentered illegally, which is a felony. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him again and issued a final order of removal. The agency said he got back into the country at an unknown time and place. “Ryan O’Shea was just 21 years old,” said acting ICE Director David J. Venturella. “He was a college student, a hockey player and a young man preparing for a career protecting others. His family should be celebrating his accomplishments and looking forward to his future. Instead, they’re mourning a life tragically cut short. We extend our deepest condolences to Ryan’s family, friends and teammates. His death is a devastating loss, and he deserves to be remembered for the life he lived and the future he was working so hard to build.” O’Shea was a senior at the University of New Haven and an assistant captain on the school’s club hockey team. He was heading home from a game, and he was studying to become a police officer. The university held a remembrance for O’Shea in October and unveiled a plaque with his name on campus. “I think it’s good that they made the arrest, I think it’s necessary and hopefully provide closure to the family and to us on campus here,” said Jack Winzer, a University of New Haven freshman. Police are still investigating the crash. They have not said where they believe Carmona-Lopez got on I-91. He passed a number of cars going the wrong way before the collision. title: Boston College Overcomes Poor Shooting, Defeats UNH 67-55 - Yahoo Sports
content: On Sunday afternoon, Boston College defeated UNH 67-55 to improve to 4-0 on the young season. New Hampshire jumped out to a quick 13-2 lead over the first 4:50 of the game, with BC's early-season shooting struggles continuing. The Eagles—missing star guard Money Williams, who per ESPN's Jeff Borzello is game-to-game—missed seven of their first eight shots. A couple threes from Ernest Shelton kept the Eagles afloat, who also welcomed back UConn transfer Jacob Furphy for his first appearance in an Eagles jersey. By the 10-minute mark, the Eagles had trimmed the deficit to one; a Zak Smrekar and-one layup at 8:12 gave BC their first lead. Furphy drilled a wing three for his first points in an Eagle uniform, and Smrekar cleaned up a Furphy missed layup on the next possession as BC's offense found a bit of a rhythm. UNH, however, continued to stay hot from beyond the arc to stay within reach. The Wildcats hit four of their first nine treys, fueling their offense. BC's Ernest Shelton—billed as a sniper after an offseason transfer from Merrimack despite early-season inconsistency—continued his hot half with back-to-back triples late in the half to put BC up 31-28 at half (despite shooting a putrid 33% from the floor). The second half began much as the first half ended: with both teams trading buckets. Luke Hunger connected from close range to briefly push BC's lead to five, but UNH answered with an immediate lay of their own. A quick 9-0 run five minutes into the second half, sparked by Shelton's fifth three and a Smrekar bucket, helped the Eagles pad their lead to double-digits. BC's offense, while far from perfect, was able to generate enough clean looks to keep UNH at bay. The amount of misses, however, was definitely concerning; Zak Smrekar and Jacob Furphy combined to shoot for 9-27 today. Despite the poor shooting, BC's defense, ability to manufacture extra possessions, and timely rebounding afforded BC a roughly 10-point lead for the last quarter of the game. Smrekar connected on his first trey with 2:43 left in the game to put BC up 13, and BC went on to seal the 67-55 win.
